lesson.title: Buy Now, Pay Later: The Rise of 1920s Consumer Culture
lesson.summary: The 1920s saw an explosion of consumer spending, advertising, and installment buying, as industrial mass production met a newly prosperous middle class eager for the latest household goods.
lesson.body:
The war that ended with the Treaty of Versailles had transformed the American economy in ways few predicted. While the fighting had devastated European farms, factories, and finances, the United States emerged from the conflict with its industrial base intact and vastly expanded. European nations now owed enormous war debts to American banks, and the United States shifted from a debtor nation to the world's leading creditor and industrial power. That industrial capacity, built up to supply the war effort, now turned to something new: producing consumer goods for American households on a massive scale.

Factories that had learned the techniques of mass production during wartime applied those same efficiencies to peacetime goods. Refrigerators, washing machines, vacuum cleaners, toasters, and radios poured out of American factories at falling prices, and for the first time these appliances became realistic purchases for millions of middle class families, not just the wealthy. Wages for many industrial and white collar workers rose during the decade, giving families more disposable income, though prosperity was far from evenly shared, and farmers in particular struggled with falling crop prices throughout the 1920s.

Two innovations made this new consumption possible. The first was modern advertising, which grew into a sophisticated industry that used psychology, celebrity endorsement, and eye catching imagery in magazines, newspapers, and later radio to convince Americans that new products were not luxuries but necessities. The second was installment buying, a system that let families purchase expensive items like automobiles and appliances by paying in small monthly amounts rather than the full price upfront. By the end of the decade a majority of major purchases, from cars to furniture, were bought on credit. This combination of mass production, aggressive advertising, and easy credit created a self reinforcing cycle of spending that defined the decade's culture and helped fuel the era's most visible symbol of consumer prosperity, the automobile.
